cases.title: Liver Cirrhosis — Abdominal Short Case
cases.summary: Examination of an adult with chronic liver disease: peripheral stigmata, ascites and portal hypertension.

signs.name: Scleral jaundice
signs.what: Yellow discolouration of the sclerae, best seen in natural light.
signs.how: Ask the patient to look up and down while you gently retract the lower lids; inspect the sclerae in daylight, not under yellow artificial light.
signs.why: Failing hepatocytes cannot conjugate and excrete bilirubin, so it accumulates in the blood and stains the sclerae and skin.
signs.brief: Close-up of both eyes of an adult with distinct yellow sclerae, natural daylight, lower lid gently retracted, no text.

signs.name: Palmar erythema
signs.what: Redness of the thenar and hypothenar eminences, sparing the centre of the palm.
signs.how: Ask the patient to hold both hands out palms up and inspect the heels of the palms in good light; compare both sides.
signs.why: The failing liver metabolises oestrogen poorly, and raised oestrogen causes peripheral vasodilatation.
signs.brief: Palms of both hands held up, clear bright red colour over the thenar and hypothenar eminences, sparing the centre of the palm, no text.

signs.name: Leuconychia
signs.what: White nails with the nail bed appearing opaque white, usually in more than one nail.
signs.how: Inspect all ten nails against a plain background; look for a uniformly white nail plate.
signs.why: Low serum albumin from reduced hepatic synthesis changes the nail bed and produces the white appearance.
signs.brief: Close-up of fingernails that are uniformly opaque white, adult hand on a plain background, no text.

signs.name: Finger clubbing
signs.what: Loss of the angle between the nail and the nail fold, with a bulbous fingertip.
signs.how: Look at the fingers from the side for loss of the nail-fold angle; check for the Schamroth window sign by placing the nails of opposing fingers together.
signs.why: Seen in cirrhosis through poorly understood vascular changes, including hepatopulmonary shunting. It is non-specific.
signs.brief: Side view of a clubbed finger showing loss of the nail-fold angle and a bulbous tip, no text.

signs.name: Dupuytren's contracture
signs.what: Thickening and puckering of the palmar fascia with fixed flexion of the ring finger, and sometimes the little finger.
signs.how: Inspect the palm for puckered skin and cords; feel the palmar fascia for nodules or a firm cord, and ask whether the fingers will straighten.
signs.why: Associated with chronic alcohol excess and liver disease, although the mechanism is not clear. It is not specific to the liver.
signs.brief: Open palm showing a tight fibrous cord running to a flexed ring finger with puckered palmar skin, no text.

signs.name: Asterixis (flapping tremor)
signs.what: A coarse, irregular flapping of the outstretched hands, a sign of hepatic encephalopathy.
signs.how: Ask the patient to stretch both arms out with the wrists dorsiflexed and fingers spread for 30 seconds; watch for a sudden loss of posture followed by a quick correction.
signs.why: Raised ammonia and other toxins that the liver no longer clears impair the brain's control of sustained posture.
signs.brief: Both arms stretched out in front, wrists dorsiflexed and fingers spread, examination room, no text.

signs.name: Spider naevi
signs.what: Central red arteriole with fine radiating vessels that blanch on pressure. Five or more is significant.
signs.how: Inspect the upper trunk, neck, face and arms. Press on the centre with a pin head or glass slide; the lesion blanches and refills from the centre.
signs.why: Raised oestrogen levels, because the liver clears it poorly, cause dilatation of cutaneous arterioles.
signs.brief: Upper chest of an adult with several small red lesions, each a central dot with radiating fine vessels, no text.

signs.name: Gynaecomastia
signs.what: Palpable breast tissue in a male, usually bilateral.
signs.how: With consent, inspect the chest from the front and then palpate behind the nipple for a firm, rubbery disc of glandular tissue, not just fat.
signs.why: A rise in the oestrogen to androgen ratio, from poor hepatic clearance of oestrogen, stimulates breast tissue. Spironolactone can also cause it.
signs.brief: Front view of a male chest with bilateral breast enlargement, clinical lighting, no text.

signs.name: Abdominal distension with ascites
signs.what: A uniformly distended abdomen with bulging flanks and, in tense ascites, an everted umbilicus.
signs.how: Stand at the foot of the bed and then at the side with the patient lying flat; look at the contour of the flanks, the umbilicus and the skin for stretch marks.
signs.why: Portal hypertension together with low albumin and sodium retention allows fluid to accumulate in the peritoneal cavity.
signs.brief: Supine adult with a distended, tense abdomen, bulging flanks and an everted umbilicus, no text.

signs.name: Caput medusae
signs.what: Dilated veins radiating from the umbilicus across the abdominal wall.
signs.how: Expose the abdomen and inspect the skin around the umbilicus. Occlude a vein and see the direction of flow if asked; in caput, flow is away from the umbilicus.
signs.why: Raised portal pressure reopens the paraumbilical veins, which connect the portal and systemic circulations.
signs.brief: Anterior abdominal wall with prominent dilated veins radiating from the umbilicus, no text.

signs.name: Liver edge and size
signs.what: In established cirrhosis the liver is often small and hard; it may be palpable with a nodular, firm edge, particularly in early or alcoholic disease.
signs.how: With the patient supine and knees slightly bent, start in the right iliac fossa and palpate upwards with the flat of the fingers, timing your movement with breathing; then percuss the upper border to estimate size.
signs.why: Fibrosis and nodular regeneration distort and, over time, shrink the liver, and it feels firm.
signs.brief: Examiner's hand palpating the right upper quadrant of a supine adult, no text.

signs.name: Splenomegaly
signs.what: A palpable spleen tip below the left costal margin that moves down on inspiration.
signs.how: Begin palpating in the right iliac fossa and move diagonally towards the left costal margin on each breath; roll the patient onto the right side and repeat.
signs.why: Portal hypertension causes back-pressure into the splenic vein and congestion of the spleen.
signs.brief: Examiner's hand palpating beneath the left costal margin of a supine adult, no text.

signs.name: Fluid thrill
signs.what: A tap on one flank is transmitted as a ripple to the opposite flank through free fluid.
signs.how: Ask the patient or an assistant to rest the edge of a hand firmly along the midline; place one palm on a flank and flick the opposite flank with a finger of the other hand.
signs.why: The ripple travels through free peritoneal fluid, so it indicates a large volume of ascites.
signs.brief: Examiner demonstrating the fluid thrill on a supine adult, with an assistant's hand on the midline, no text.

signs.name: Shifting dullness
signs.what: Dullness in the flanks that moves to the uppermost flank when the patient rolls onto their side.
signs.how: Percuss from the midline towards a flank until the note turns dull, keep your finger there, ask the patient to roll away, wait 30 seconds, and percuss again.
signs.why: Free fluid settles to the dependent flank and bowel loops float to the top, so the note changes with position.
signs.brief: Examiner percussing the flank of a supine adult, abdomen exposed, no text.

signs.name: Pitting oedema
signs.what: Indentation left in the skin of the shins and ankles after firm pressure.
signs.how: Press firmly with your thumb over the tibia for at least five seconds and look for an indentation; note how high the swelling extends and check the sacrum.
signs.why: Low albumin reduces oncotic pressure, and sodium and water retention adds to it, so fluid leaks into the tissues.
signs.brief: Both lower legs of an adult with swelling and a visible thumb-print indentation over the shin, no text.

chain.title: Chronic liver injury
chain.body: Long-standing injury from alcohol, chronic hepatitis B or C or fatty liver disease leads to inflammation and the deposition of scar tissue.

chain.title: Fibrosis and portal hypertension
chain.body: Scarring and nodular regeneration distort the liver's architecture and raise resistance to portal flow, so pressure in the portal venous system rises and collaterals open.

chain.title: Falling liver function
chain.body: Fewer working hepatocytes means less albumin and clotting factors, poor clearance of oestrogen and bilirubin, and less detoxification of ammonia.

chain.title: Fluid retention
chain.body: Low albumin, portal hypertension and sodium retention push fluid into the peritoneal cavity and the tissues, causing ascites and oedema.

chain.title: Encephalopathy
chain.body: Toxins that the liver no longer clears, mainly ammonia, and portosystemic shunting affect the brain and cause confusion, a reversed sleep pattern and asterixis.

findings: Raised AST and ALT, with AST:ALT above 2 suggesting alcohol
Raised ALP and GGT may be present
Prolonged prothrombin time and INR reflecting poor synthetic function
Dilated portal vein and collaterals on Doppler
Neutrophil count above 250 per mm3 indicates spontaneous bacterial peritonitis
Serum-ascites albumin gradient of 11 g/L or more suggests portal hypertension

keyPoints: Cirrhosis is irreversible scarring with nodular regeneration; its consequences are portal hypertension and failing liver function.
Examine hands, face, chest, abdomen and legs in that order.
Ascites is confirmed by shifting dullness; a large volume also gives a fluid thrill.
Always look for signs of decompensation: jaundice, ascites, asterixis.
osceTips: Tell the examiner what you are looking for as you go, for example 'I am checking for asterixis'.
Expose the abdomen from nipple line to the groin with the patient covered below.
Say 'chronic liver disease' first; name cirrhosis only once you can justify portal hypertension or decompensation.

items: Assess airway, breathing and circulation and look for bleeding, sepsis and confusion.
Check glucose, U&E, liver tests, clotting and blood cultures; examine for ascites and peritonitis.
Do a diagnostic ascitic tap in any patient admitted with ascites.
Variceal bleeding: resuscitate, give a vasoactive drug and antibiotics, and arrange urgent endoscopy.
Ascites: restrict dietary sodium and use spironolactone, with a loop diuretic if needed; therapeutic paracentesis for tense ascites.
Spontaneous bacterial peritonitis: antibiotics and albumin.
Hepatic encephalopathy: treat the trigger and give lactulose.
Treat the cause: alcohol abstinence, antivirals for hepatitis B or C, weight loss for fatty liver disease.
Ultrasound surveillance for hepatocellular carcinoma about every six months.
Endoscopic screening for varices and non-selective beta-blocker or band ligation as indicated.
Vaccination and nutritional support; consider referral for liver transplantation.

questions.q: Name four causes of chronic liver disease that lead to cirrhosis.
questions.a: Alcohol, chronic hepatitis B or C, non-alcoholic fatty liver disease and autoimmune or genetic causes such as primary biliary cholangitis, haemochromatosis and Wilson's disease.

questions.q: What is shifting dullness and what does it mean?
questions.a: Dullness to percussion in the flanks that moves to the uppermost flank when the patient rolls; it indicates free fluid, that is, ascites.

questions.q: What are the complications of cirrhosis you would look for?
questions.a: Variceal bleeding, ascites with spontaneous bacterial peritonitis, hepatic encephalopathy, hepatorenal syndrome, coagulopathy and hepatocellular carcinoma.
